props.title: The Blair Witch Project
props.initialSlug: Lost in the woods, terror awaits.

sections.content: The Blair Witch Project revolutionized horror filmmaking and launched the found footage genre into the mainstream. Shot for just $60,000, it grossed $248 million by convincing audiences they were watching real recovered footage. The film's viral marketing campaign - including fake documentaries and missing person posters - created the first major internet movie phenomenon. Directors Daniel Myrick and Eduardo Sánchez proved that shaky cameras, unknown actors, and unseen threats could terrify more effectively than big-budget special effects.

sections.content: The success of Blair Witch spawned countless imitators but few captured its raw authenticity. Cloverfield (2008) applied the handheld approach to a monster movie, while Lake Mungo (2008) used mock documentary interviews to build crushing dread. Host (2020) proved the format could still innovate by setting its supernatural horror entirely within a Zoom call during lockdown.

Found footage evolved beyond horror with films like Chronicle (2012) tackling superhero origin stories and End of Watch (2012) bringing visceral immediacy to police drama. But horror remained the genre's sweet spot, with standouts like Trollhunter (2010) and Hell House LLC (2015) finding fresh angles on familiar monsters. SUBHEAD: Documentary Horror Evolution

sections.content: The blurred line between fact and fiction that made The Blair Witch Project so effective inspired a wave of horror films masquerading as documentaries. Lake Mungo (2008) uses interviews, photos, and home videos to investigate a drowning death with supernatural undertones. The Taking of Deborah Logan (2014) begins as a medical documentary about Alzheimer's before descending into possession horror. These films leverage documentary techniques to ground their supernatural elements in reality.

Modern found footage continues to evolve through technological innovation. Searching (2018) tells its story entirely through computer screens and smartphones. Unfriended (2014) unfolds in real-time via Skype calls and social media. These films reflect how our relationship with recording devices and screens has changed since Blair Witch's camcorder days.
